Loss of motor function, pain, and temperature bilaterally below the lesion; preserved vibration and proprioception
Loss of only proprioception and vibration

rationale.text: Anterior spinal artery syndrome destroys anterior 2/3 of cord: bilateral corticospinal tracts (motor loss) and lateral spinothalamic tracts (pain/temp loss), but spares the dorsal columns (vibration/proprioception preserved).

subject: Anatomy
question: The basal ganglia circuit is involved in which function, and which nucleus is most affected in Huntington's disease?

rationale.text: The basal ganglia are involved in voluntary motor control. Huntington's disease preferentially affects the caudate nucleus (along with putamen), causing loss of GABA-ergic neurons.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which brainstem structure is responsible for the coordination of eye movements and is affected in internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)?

rationale.text: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) connects CN VI on one side to CN III on the other to coordinate lateral gaze. Demyelination (e.g., MS) of the MLF causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient with Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome will present with which combination of deficits?
options: Ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss + contralateral body pain/temperature loss + ipsilateral Horner's + dysphagia
Contralateral hemiplegia + ipsilateral CN III palsy
Ipsilateral facial weakness + contralateral arm/leg weakness
Bilateral arm weakness and bilateral Babinski

rationale.text: Wallenberg (PICA occlusion) syndrome: ipsilateral face pain/temp loss (V nucleus), contralateral body pain/temp loss (spinothalamic), ipsilateral Horner's, dysarthria, dysphagia, vertigo.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient with a lesion of the left posterior limb of the internal capsule will have motor deficits on which side?

rationale.text: The corticospinal tract decussates in the medullary pyramids. A left internal capsule lesion produces right-sided spastic hemiplegia (contralateral to the lesion).

subject: Anatomy
question: Which type of aphasia is characterized by non-fluent speech, poor repetition, but relatively intact comprehension?

rationale.text: Broca's aphasia: non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension. Patients know what they want to say but cannot produce it. Lesion in inferior frontal gyrus.

subject: Anatomy
question: Syringomyelia causes a characteristic 'cape-like' distribution of sensory loss. Which modality is lost first, and why?
options: Proprioception; dorsal columns are compressed first
Pain and temperature in bilateral upper extremities; anterior commissure fibers are disrupted as the syrinx expands
Fine touch; spinothalamic decussation is interrupted
All modalities equally; the cord is uniformly compressed

rationale.text: A syrinx (fluid-filled cavity) expands centrally and disrupts the crossing spinothalamic fibers at the anterior commissure, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature in the upper extremities ('cape' distribution). Dorsal columns (proprioception) are initially spared.

subject: Anatomy
question: The left-right body axis during embryonic development is established by which key signaling pathway first activated at the node?
options: Nodal (TGF-β family) is expressed on the LEFT, establishing left-sided identity
BMP-4 expression on the right establishes right identity
Sonic hedgehog acts bilaterally to establish symmetry
Wnt signaling establishes left-right asymmetry independent of cilia

rationale.text: Nodal cilia at the node create leftward fluid flow → Nodal expression on the LEFT → activates Pitx2 (transcription factor for left-sided organogenesis). Lefty inhibits and confines Nodal signaling.

subject: Anatomy
question: The nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc is a remnant of which embryologic structure?

rationale.text: The nucleus pulposus is a remnant of the embryonic notochord, which induces neural tube development and serves as the initial axial skeleton scaffold.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which dermatome corresponds to the umbilicus (a key landmark for dermatome mapping)?

rationale.text: T10 corresponds to the umbilicus. T4 = nipple, T6 = xiphoid, T10 = umbilicus, T12 = inguinal fold, L1 = inguinal ligament, L4 = knee.

subject: Anatomy
question: Phalen's test (holding wrists in forced flexion) reproduces symptoms in which condition?

rationale.text: Phalen's test compresses the carpal tunnel by forced wrist flexion for 60 seconds, reproducing median nerve symptoms (numbness/tingling in lateral 3½ fingers) in carpal tunnel syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient presents with 'Saturday night palsy'—wrist drop after sleeping with the arm over a chair back. Which nerve is compressed, and at which specific location?
options: Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel
Radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus
Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
Axillary nerve at the surgical neck of the humerus

rationale.text: Saturday night palsy compresses the radial nerve in the spiral groove (mid-humerus), typically from prolonged pressure against the humerus. It causes wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand, sparing the brachioradialis and sensation over the posterior arm (branches arise more proximally).

subject: Anatomy
question: A newborn has an open neural tube defect at the lumbar level with exposed spinal cord. Which embryonic event failed?

rationale.text: Myelomeningocele (spina bifida cystica) results from failure of neural fold fusion during neurulation (3rd–4th week). The neural tube fails to close, leaving the spinal cord exposed.

subject: Anatomy
question: A neonate has anencephaly. Which embryonic failure is responsible?
options: Failure of caudal neural tube closure
Failure of rostral (anterior) neural tube closure

rationale.text: Anencephaly results from failure of the anterior (rostral) neuropore to close by day 25. The brain and calvarium fail to develop. Maternal folic acid deficiency is a major risk factor.

subject: Anatomy
question: The apical ectodermal ridge (AER) drives limb bud outgrowth. If the AER is removed, what results?
options: Limb is truncated at the level corresponding to the developmental stage

rationale.text: The AER provides signals (FGFs) for proximal-to-distal outgrowth of the limb bud. Removal at any stage truncates the limb at the level of development reached at that point (proximal structures already formed, distal ones absent).

subject: Anatomy
question: The zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) at the posterior limb bud margin establishes which axis?

rationale.text: The zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) secretes Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) to establish the anterior-posterior (pre-axial to post-axial / thumb to little finger) axis of limb development.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which embryonic structure gives rise to the epithelium of both the anterior 2/3 and posterior 1/3 of the tongue?
options: 2nd arch for anterior 2/3 and 4th arch for posterior 1/3
Neural crest cells for the entire tongue

rationale.text: The anterior 2/3 of the tongue epithelium arises from the 1st pharyngeal arch (innervated by V3 for general sensation, VII for taste via chorda tympani). The posterior 1/3 arises from the 3rd arch (innervated by IX for both sensation and taste).

subject: Anatomy
question: A 55-year-old man has ipsilateral Horner syndrome, contralateral loss of pain and temperature, ipsilateral ataxia, and ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss. Which syndrome is this?

rationale.text: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary/PICA syndrome): ipsilateral Horner's (sympathetic chain), ipsilateral facial pain/temp loss (spinal trigeminal nucleus), contralateral body pain/temp loss (spinothalamic tract), ipsilateral ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle), dysphagia (nucleus ambiguus).

subject: Anatomy
question: A 45-year-old man has a T6 spinal cord hemisection. On the right: loss of fine touch and vibration; on the left: loss of pain and temperature below T6. Which syndrome is this?

rationale.text: Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection): ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception (dorsal columns); ipsilateral UMN signs (corticospinal tract); contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract, which crosses within 1–2 levels of entry).

subject: Anatomy
question: A 40-year-old with acute cervical disc herniation has bilateral arm weakness worse than leg weakness, with a cape-like loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders. Which spinal cord syndrome is this?

rationale.text: Central cord syndrome: injury to the central gray matter and adjacent crossing spinothalamic fibers. Upper extremity weakness > lower extremity (arm fibers more central in corticospinal tract), cape-like bilateral loss of pain/temp (crossing fibers), bladder dysfunction. Most common in elderly with cervical spondylosis.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 30-year-old diver sustains a hyperflexion injury and has bilateral loss of motor function and pain/temperature sensation below the level, with preserved proprioception. Which syndrome?

rationale.text: Anterior cord syndrome: damage to the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord (corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts), sparing the dorsal columns. Bilateral loss of motor function and pain/temperature with preserved fine touch, vibration, and proprioception.

subject: Anatomy
question: The dorsal (posterior) column–medial lemniscal pathway carries which sensory modalities?
options: Fine touch, vibration, proprioception, and 2-point discrimination

rationale.text: The dorsal column–medial lemniscal system carries fine (discriminative) touch, vibration, proprioception, and 2-point discrimination. Fibers ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns and decussate in the medulla at the level of the nucleus gracilis/cuneatus.

subject: Anatomy
question: The spinothalamic tract carries which sensory modalities and where does it decussate?
options: Fine touch; decussates in the medulla
Pain and temperature; decussates within 1–2 spinal levels of entry (anterior white commissure)

rationale.text: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature. Afferents synapse in the dorsal horn, then cross in the anterior white commissure within 1–2 spinal segments before ascending in the contralateral lateral funiculus to the thalamus.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 60-year-old diabetic has a cervical myelopathy causing bilateral leg spasticity and hyperreflexia. Which tract is most affected?

rationale.text: Bilateral spasticity and hyperreflexia (UMN signs) below the lesion indicate bilateral lateral corticospinal tract compression — the hallmark of cervical myelopathy.

subject: Anatomy
question: Syringomyelia causes a cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch. Which fibers are disrupted first?
options: Anterior white commissure crossing spinothalamic fibers

rationale.text: Syringomyelia expands from within the central canal, first disrupting the anterior white commissure where pain and temperature fibers cross — causing a bilateral, symmetric, cape-like (shawl) distribution of loss. Dorsal columns are spared until late.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which thalamic nucleus relays pain and temperature from the face?

rationale.text: The VPM (ventral posteromedial) nucleus of the thalamus relays pain, temperature, and tactile sensation from the face (via trigeminal pathway). VPL relays the same modalities from the body.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 25-year-old has severe low back pain after a fall. MRI shows massive L4–L5 disc herniation compressing multiple nerve roots. He has perianal numbness, urinary retention, and bilateral leg weakness with absent reflexes. What is this syndrome?

rationale.text: Cauda equina syndrome (compression of the nerve roots below L1–L2 where the cord ends) presents with LMN signs: flaccid paralysis, areflexia, saddle anesthesia (S3–S5), and sphincter dysfunction (urinary retention, fecal incontinence). A surgical emergency.

subject: Anatomy
question: The gracile fasciculus carries proprioception from which part of the body?
options: Upper limb and trunk above T6
Lower limb and trunk below T6

rationale.text: The gracile fasciculus (medial dorsal column) carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from the lower limb and trunk below T6. The cuneate fasciculus (lateral dorsal column) carries the same from the upper limb and trunk above T6.

subject: Anatomy
question: At which anatomical level do approximately 85% of corticospinal tract fibers cross to the contralateral side?
options: Posterior limb of the internal capsule
Caudal medulla at the medullospinal junction

rationale.text: The corticospinal tract fibers decussate at the pyramidal decussation at the caudal medulla (medullospinal junction), where approximately 85% cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract. The remaining 15% descend ipsilaterally as the anterior corticospinal tract.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 70-year-old man has a lesion of the right internal capsule. Which side of the body shows contralateral UMN signs?

rationale.text: A right internal capsule lesion interrupts the corticospinal fibers before they decussate at the pyramidal decussation. The resulting UMN signs (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) appear contralaterally (left side of the body). The face shows contralateral lower face weakness (upper motor neuron facial palsy).

subject: Anatomy
question: A 50-year-old woman has carpal tunnel syndrome. Which nerve is compressed, and at which location?
options: Median nerve under the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament)
Radial nerve at the radial groove
Anterior interosseous nerve at the pronator teres
Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel

rationale.text: Carpal tunnel syndrome involves compression of the median nerve under the flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament) at the wrist, causing thenar atrophy, loss of opposition, and sensory loss in the lateral 3.5 digits.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which muscle is the only flexor of the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger supplied exclusively by the median nerve?
options: Flexor digitorum profundus (lateral half — index and middle)

rationale.text: The lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus (supplying the index and middle finger DIP flexion) is innervated by the anterior interosseous nerve (branch of median nerve). Testing FDP of the index finger specifically tests the median nerve at the forearm level.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 40-year-old woman has a winging of the scapula. Which nerve is injured and which muscle is denervated?

rationale.text: Medial (classic) scapular winging is caused by injury to the long thoracic nerve (C5–C7), denervating the serratus anterior. The scapula loses its stabilization against the chest wall and 'wings' posteromedially, especially on shoulder elevation.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 20-year-old rugby player has an anterior shoulder dislocation. Which nerve is most at risk?

rationale.text: The axillary nerve passes posterior to the surgical neck of the humerus and through the quadrangular space. It is the most commonly injured nerve in anterior shoulder dislocations, causing deltoid weakness and loss of sensation over the 'regimental badge' area of the lateral upper arm.

subject: Anatomy
question: Thoracic outlet syndrome most commonly compresses which component of the brachial plexus?

rationale.text: Thoracic outlet syndrome most commonly compresses the lower trunk (C8–T1), producing wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles, sensory loss in the medial forearm and hand (ulnar distribution), and ipsilateral Horner's syndrome if sympathetic fibers are involved.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient has an Erb-Duchenne palsy after a difficult birth. Which nerve roots are involved, and what is the classic posture?
options: C5–C6; 'waiter's tip' posture (arm internally rotated, extended, pronated, wrist flexed)

rationale.text: Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5–C6 injury) from excessive lateral flexion/traction: deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, biceps, and brachioradialis denervation → 'waiter's tip' posture (arm adducted, internally rotated, extended, forearm pronated, wrist flexed).

subject: Anatomy
question: A 35-year-old runner has lower leg pain and weakness on dorsiflexion after prolonged exercise. Pressure in the anterior compartment is elevated. Which nerve is at risk in anterior compartment syndrome of the leg?

rationale.text: The anterior compartment of the leg contains the deep fibular nerve. Compartment syndrome compresses this nerve, causing foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion) and loss of sensation in the first web space.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 65-year-old man has tarsal tunnel syndrome causing burning pain on the medial foot and sole. Which nerve is compressed?
options: Tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel

rationale.text: Tarsal tunnel syndrome involves compression of the tibial nerve (or its branches: medial and lateral plantar nerves) as it passes through the tarsal tunnel (flexor retinaculum) posterior to the medial malleolus.

subject: Anatomy
question: The L4 dermatome corresponds to which surface area for clinical testing?
options: Dorsum of foot and great toe

rationale.text: The L4 dermatome covers the medial leg and medial malleolus. The L4 myotome tests knee extension (quadriceps) and ankle dorsiflexion/inversion. Loss of the patellar reflex indicates L4 involvement.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which dermatome covers the dorsum of the foot and great toe, and is tested by which reflex?

rationale.text: L5 dermatomal territory includes the dorsum of the foot and great toe. The L5 myotome tests great toe extension (extensor hallucis longus) and foot eversion. There is no reliable deep tendon reflex for L5 (the posterior tibialis reflex is inconsistent).

subject: Anatomy
question: Which dermatome covers the lateral foot and little toe, and corresponds to which reflex?

rationale.text: S1 supplies the lateral foot, little toe, and posterior calf. The Achilles (ankle jerk) reflex tests S1. Loss of S1 indicates L5–S1 disc herniation (the most common level), causing plantar flexion weakness and diminished Achilles reflex.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which muscle's dysfunction causes a Trendelenburg gait (pelvis drops on the contralateral side during single-leg stance)?
options: Gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve)

rationale.text: Trendelenburg gait: failure of the gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve, L4–S1) to stabilize the pelvis causes the unsupported side to drop during single-leg stance. The body compensates by shifting the trunk over the affected limb (compensated Trendelenburg).

subject: Anatomy
question: A 55-year-old man wakes up with complete right-sided facial weakness involving the forehead, inability to close his eye, and drooping of the corner of his mouth. Which type of lesion explains equal involvement of the upper and lower face?
options: Lower motor neuron peripheral nerve lesion
Lesion at the facial nerve nucleus only
Fascicular lesion at the genu of the facial nerve

rationale.text: Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of CN VII (Bell's palsy) causes ipsilateral complete facial weakness including forehead (frontalis), eye closure (orbicularis oculi), and lower face. UMN lesions spare the forehead (bilateral cortical representation).

subject: Anatomy
question: The cavernous sinus contains which cranial nerves and other structures?
options: CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI; internal carotid artery
CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI, internal carotid artery, and sympathetic plexus around ICA
CN V1, V2, V3, VII, and internal carotid artery
CN III, IV, V, VI, VII, and internal jugular vein
CN III, V1, V2, and vertebral artery

rationale.text: The cavernous sinus contains: CN III (oculomotor), CN IV (trochlear), CN V1 (ophthalmic), CN V2 (maxillary) — in lateral wall; CN VI (abducens) — runs through the sinus adjacent to the ICA; and the internal carotid artery with its sympathetic plexus. CN VI is most vulnerable to mass lesions within the sinus.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which dural venous sinus runs in the superior border of the tentorium cerebelli and drains into the confluence of sinuses?

rationale.text: The transverse sinuses run in the attached margin of the tentorium cerebelli from the confluence of sinuses (torcula Herophili) to the sigmoid sinuses, which drain into the internal jugular veins at the jugular foramina.

subject: Anatomy
question: In the SCALP mnemonic, one layer is considered the 'danger zone' because infections there can spread intracranially via valveless emissary veins. Which layer is this?

rationale.text: The loose areolar tissue (4th layer of SCALP) is the 'danger zone' — infections spread freely through this layer and can drain via emissary veins (which have no valves) into the intracranial dural sinuses, risking cavernous sinus thrombosis or meningitis.

subject: Anatomy
question: The contents of the superior orbital fissure include which cranial nerves?
options: CN II, III, IV, V1, VI
CN III, IV, V1 (ophthalmic), VI, superior ophthalmic vein, sympathetic fibers
CN II, VI, and sympathetic fibers

rationale.text: Superior orbital fissure transmits: CN III (oculomotor), CN IV (trochlear), CN V1 — nasociliary and frontal branches (ophthalmic), CN VI (abducens), superior ophthalmic vein, and sympathetic fibers. The optic canal separately transmits CN II and ophthalmic artery.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient has a 'blown pupil' (fixed dilated pupil) after head trauma with a subdural hematoma. Which cranial nerve is compressed by uncal herniation?
options: CN II at the optic chiasm
CN III (oculomotor) at the tentorial notch
CN VI in the cavernous sinus
CN IV at the trochlear notch
CN V at the trigeminal cave

rationale.text: Uncal herniation compresses CN III (oculomotor nerve) at the tentorial notch, interrupting parasympathetic fibers (which run on the outside of the nerve) first — causing ipsilateral mydriasis (blown pupil) before motor deficits. This is a neurosurgical emergency.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient was accidentally hit by a car on his left leg. He now comes to the clinic complaining of loss of sensation on the dorsal aspect of his left foot and inability to lift the foot while walking resulting to a 'steppage gait'. What is the most likely injured nerve?

rationale.text: Injury to the common peroneal nerve leads to foot drop ('steppage gait') and loss of dorsal foot sensation. Mnemonic: PED (Peroneal Everts and Dorsiflexes).

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient was brought to the ER for a possible disc herniation. On examination, there was noted weakness of knee extension and decreased patellar reflex. What is the most likely nerve root affected?

rationale.text: Disc herniation that affects the L4 nerve root leads to weakness of knee extension and decreased patellar reflex.

subject: Anatomy
question: Injury to the surgical neck of the humerus will damage which of the following nerves?

rationale.text: Injury to the surgical neck of the humerus leads to injury of the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex artery.

subject: Anatomy
question: What artery is involved with injury to the midshaft of the humerus?

rationale.text: Injury to the midshaft of the humerus injures the radial nerve and deep brachial artery.

subject: Anatomy
question: An elderly patient with osteoporosis suffers a right posterior hip dislocation. Which of the following nerves is most likely injured in this case?

rationale.text: The inferior gluteal nerve innervates the gluteus maximus and is associated with posterior hip dislocations.

subject: Anatomy
question: Cerebrospinal fluid made in the choroid plexus flows into the 4th ventricle from the 3rd ventricle via the

rationale.text: CSF flow: Lateral ventricles -> Foramina of Monro -> 3rd ventricle -> Aqueduct of Sylvius -> 4th ventricle.

subject: Anatomy
question: Taste sensation from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is carried by which of the following cranial nerves?

rationale.text: Taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is carried by chorda tympani which is a branch of CN VII.

subject: Anatomy
question: The following are the contents of the carotid sheath, EXCEPT?

rationale.text: The contents of the carotid sheath are: Common and internal carotid arteries, Internal jugular vein, and Vagus nerve. The external jugular vein is not inside the sheath.

subject: Anatomy
question: The 5 secondary vesicles are the telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, and myelencephalon. The basal ganglia develops from which of those 5?

rationale.text: Telencephalon forms the cerebral hemispheres and basal ganglia.

subject: Anatomy
question: What is the largest and most abundant glial cell in the CNS?

rationale.text: Astrocytes are the largest and most abundant glial cells in the central nervous system.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which of the following cells originated from the mesoderm?

rationale.text: Microglia originate from the mesoderm. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes originate from neural tube (ectoderm).

subject: Anatomy
question: Which of the following tracts in the spinal cord is responsible for voluntary and motor function?

rationale.text: The corticospinal tracts are responsible for voluntary motor function.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which hypothalamic area is involved in increasing appetite?

rationale.text: The lateral area of the hypothalamus is known as the hunger center and is involved in increasing appetite.

subject: Anatomy
question: An infection in which layer of the scalp is associated with increased risk of spreading to the intracranial sinuses via the emissary veins?

rationale.text: The loose connective tissue layer of the scalp is the 'danger zone' where infection can spread to intracranial sinuses via emissary veins.

subject: Anatomy
question: A fracture sustained at the thinnest area of the lateral skull will result in rupture of which of the following vessels?

rationale.text: The pterion is the thinnest part of the lateral skull. A fracture here can rupture the middle meningeal artery resulting in an epidural hematoma.

subject: Anatomy
question: Eliciting the patellar reflex results in contraction of which muscle?

rationale.text: Eliciting the patellar reflex results in contraction of the quadriceps femoris.

subject: Anatomy
question: Dislocation of which of the following carpal bones is associated with carpal tunnel syndrome?

rationale.text: Lunate dislocation can impinge the median nerve, leading to carpal tunnel syndrome.

subject: Anatomy
question: The 'Hand of Benediction' sign, which occurs when the patient attempts to make a fist, is a manifestation of a lesion in which of the following?

rationale.text: A proximal median nerve lesion presents as a 'Hand of Benediction' when attempting to make a fist.

subject: Anatomy
question: Cavernous sinus thrombosis from an infection will affect all of the following structures, EXCEPT?

rationale.text: CN II does not pass through the cavernous sinus. Structures that do pass include CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI, and the internal carotid artery.

subject: Anatomy
question: The presence of Wernicke aphasia is attributed to a stroke in what artery?

rationale.text: An MCA (Middle Cerebral Artery) stroke most likely presents with Wernicke aphasia if it affects the dominant temporal lobe.

subject: Anatomy
question: The chorda tympani nerve carries which functional component?
options: Special visceral afferent (taste from posterior 1/3 of tongue)
General somatic afferent (touch to anterior ear)
General visceral efferent (parasympathetics to submandibular/sublingual glands) + taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue

rationale.text: The chorda tympani (branch of CN VII) carries taste from the anterior 2/3 of tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands.

subject: Anatomy
question: The Meibomian glands are located where, and their infection causes which type of stye?
options: At the eyelash follicles; external hordeolum
Within the tarsal plate; internal hordeolum (deeper, toward conjunctival side)

rationale.text: Meibomian glands are embedded in the tarsal plate. Infection causes an internal hordeolum/stye, which presents as a deeper swelling toward the conjunctival side of the eyelid.

subject: Anatomy
question: The glands of Zeis are associated with which infection?

rationale.text: Glands of Zeis are sebaceous glands associated with eyelash follicles. Their infection causes an external hordeolum (stye), which presents as superficial swelling near the eyelashes.

subject: Anatomy
question: Injury to the right optic tract causes which visual field defect?

rationale.text: The right optic tract contains fibers from the temporal retina of the right eye and nasal retina of the left eye, representing the left visual field. Lesion causes left homonymous hemianopia.

subject: Anatomy
question: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus provides parasympathetic innervation for which reflex?

rationale.text: The Edinger-Westphal (accessory oculomotor) nucleus is the preganglionic parasympathetic nucleus for the ciliary ganglion, mediating pupillary constriction (miosis) via the pupillary light reflex. It also contributes to accommodation.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 68-year-old hypertensive man develops an acute ipsilateral CN III palsy (ptosis, dilated pupil, eye deviated down and out) and contralateral hemiplegia. Where is the lesion?
options: Pons at the level of CN VI and VII
Midbrain at the level of the cerebral peduncle
Posterior limb of the internal capsule

rationale.text: Weber syndrome results from a midbrain lesion involving the CN III fascicles (ipsilateral oculomotor palsy) and the adjacent cerebral peduncle (corticospinal tract — contralateral hemiplegia).

subject: Anatomy
question: Which cranial nerve provides the afferent limb of the corneal reflex, and which provides the efferent limb?
options: CN V1 (ophthalmic) afferent; CN VII (facial) efferent
CN V2 (maxillary) afferent; CN VII efferent
CN III afferent; CN VII efferent
CN V1 afferent; CN III efferent
CN VII afferent; CN V1 efferent

rationale.text: Corneal reflex: afferent = nasociliary branch of ophthalmic division (V1) of trigeminal nerve; efferent = facial nerve (CN VII) causing orbicularis oculi to blink. Testing the corneal reflex assesses both V1 and VII.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient presents with proptosis, periorbital edema, and ophthalmoplegia after a facial skin infection. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is suspected. Which cranial nerve is typically affected first, causing loss of lateral gaze?
options: CN III — causing ptosis and pupil dilation first
CN IV — causing vertical diplopia first
CN VI — causing impaired abduction first
CN V1 — causing corneal anesthesia first
CN V2 — causing midface numbness first

rationale.text: In cavernous sinus thrombosis or mass lesions, CN VI (abducens) is most vulnerable as it runs through (not just in the lateral wall of) the sinus alongside the ICA. Lateral gaze palsy (loss of abduction) is often the first oculomotor sign.

subject: Anatomy
question: What is the afferent branch of the pupillary reflex?

rationale.text: The pupillary reflex: Afferent is CN II, Efferent is CN III.

subject: Anatomy
question: What cranial nerve is responsible for eyelid opening by innervating the levator palpebrae superioris?

rationale.text: The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by CN III, which opens the eyelids.

subject: Anatomy
question: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is vulnerable to injury during which surgical procedure?

rationale.text: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch and can be damaged during aortic arch or thoracic surgery, causing hoarseness.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient undergoes thyroid surgery and develops hoarseness postoperatively. Which nerve was most likely injured?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

rationale.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of the vagus, CN X) runs close to the thyroid and is at risk during thyroid surgery. Injury causes hoarseness by paralyzing the vocal cord.

subject: Anatomy
question: Hoarseness following thyroid surgery is caused by injury to which nerve, a branch of which cranial nerve?

rationale.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus nerve (CN X). Injury during thyroidectomy is a known complication, causing ipsilateral vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness.

subject: Anatomy
question: A lesion at the optic chiasm (e.g., pituitary adenoma) causes which visual field defect?

rationale.text: The optic chiasm contains crossing nasal fibers (temporal visual fields). Compression (e.g., pituitary macroadenoma) classically causes bitemporal hemianopia ('tunnel vision').

subject: Anatomy
question: The hypothalamus controls all of the following EXCEPT:

rationale.text: Conscious proprioception is a function of the dorsal columns and somatosensory cortex, NOT the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus regulates autonomic functions, temperature, hunger, sleep, thirst, and ADH release.

subject: Anatomy
question: The first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage) gives rise to which structures?
options: Stapes, styloid process, lesser horn of hyoid
Malleus, incus, anterior ligament of malleus, sphenomandibular ligament
Greater horn of hyoid and body of hyoid

rationale.text: The first pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage) derivatives: malleus, incus, anterior ligament of malleus, sphenomandibular ligament, and the muscles of mastication (mandibular nerve, V3).

subject: Anatomy
question: The third and fourth pharyngeal pouches give rise to which endocrine/lymphoid structures?
options: 3rd pouch → thymus and inferior parathyroids; 4th pouch → superior parathyroids (and ultimobranchial body)

rationale.text: 3rd pharyngeal pouch → thymus (ventral wing) and inferior parathyroid glands (dorsal wing). 4th pharyngeal pouch → superior parathyroid glands (dorsal wing) and ultimobranchial body (parafollicular C cells of thyroid).

subject: Anatomy
question: A 3-month-old infant has hypocalcemia, T-cell deficiency, and conotruncal heart defects. Which embryonic structure failed to develop?

rationale.text: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) results from failure of development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches: absence of thymus (T-cell deficiency), absence of inferior parathyroids (hypocalcemia), and associated conotruncal heart defects.

subject: Anatomy
question: The superior parathyroid glands are derived from which pharyngeal pouch?

rationale.text: Superior parathyroid glands derive from the 4th pharyngeal pouch. Because they travel a shorter distance, they are more predictably located posterior to the upper poles of the thyroid. Inferior parathyroids come from the 3rd pouch and are more variable in position.

subject: Anatomy
question: The right adrenal gland drains directly into which vessel?

rationale.text: The right adrenal vein drains directly and very briefly into the IVC. This short course makes right adrenalectomy more challenging. The left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein.

subject: Anatomy
question: The left adrenal gland drains into which vessel?

rationale.text: The left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein (which then drains to the IVC). This is also why left-sided varicoceles are more common — the left gonadal vein similarly drains into the left renal vein at a 90° angle.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 35-year-old woman presents with episodic hypertension, headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis. Urine shows elevated metanephrines. A 4-cm adrenal mass is found on CT. Which condition follows the 'rule of 10s'?

rationale.text: Pheochromocytoma follows the 'rule of 10s': 10% bilateral, 10% malignant, 10% extra-adrenal (paragangliomas), 10% familial, 10% in children. It secretes catecholamines (epinephrine > norepinephrine from adrenal medulla).

subject: Anatomy
question: The right adrenal gland is pyramidal in shape and lies at which vertebral level?

rationale.text: The right adrenal gland (pyramidal/triangular shape) lies at T11–T12, superior to the right kidney and posterior to the IVC. The left adrenal is crescentic (semilunar) and more medial.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 30-year-old man has a hypertensive crisis, sweating, and palpitations. CT shows a 3 cm right adrenal mass. Which enzyme converts norepinephrine to epinephrine in the adrenal medulla?

rationale.text: PNMT (phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase) converts norepinephrine to epinephrine in the adrenal medulla. This reaction requires high cortisol concentrations from the adrenal cortex via the portal vasculature — explaining why adrenal medullary pheochromocytoma produces mainly epinephrine.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which is the most common neuroendocrine tumor of the gastrointestinal tract, most frequently found in the ileum?

rationale.text: Carcinoid tumor (now classified as well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor) is the most common neuroendocrine tumor of the GI tract, most often found in the small intestine (ileum), followed by the rectum and appendix.

subject: Anatomy
question: The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of which vessel?

rationale.text: The superior thyroid artery is typically the first anterior branch of the external carotid artery, supplying the upper poles of the thyroid gland and running with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

subject: Anatomy
question: The inferior thyroid artery is a branch of which vessel?

rationale.text: The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk, a branch of the subclavian artery. It supplies the lower poles of the thyroid and the parathyroid glands, and runs close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

subject: Anatomy
question: A thyroid surgeon ligates the inferior thyroid artery close to the gland. Which structure is most at risk?
options: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve

rationale.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in close proximity to the inferior thyroid artery, crossing either anterior or posterior to it. Ligation close to the gland risks injury to the RLN, causing hoarseness.

subject: Anatomy
question: At which vertebral level does the thyroid gland lie?

rationale.text: The thyroid gland lies at approximately C5–T1 vertebral levels, with the isthmus overlying the 2nd–4th tracheal rings and the upper poles reaching to C5.

subject: Anatomy
question: After thyroidectomy, a patient develops perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, and a positive Chvostek sign. Which structure was likely inadvertently removed?

rationale.text: Inadvertent removal of parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy causes hypoparathyroidism → hypocalcemia → tetany (Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm).

subject: Anatomy
question: The superior parathyroid glands lie posterior to which part of the thyroid?
options: Upper poles, posterior surface (at junction of upper and middle thirds)

rationale.text: Superior parathyroid glands lie posterior to the upper poles of the thyroid (at the junction of the upper and middle thirds), adjacent to where the inferior thyroid artery crosses the RLN. They are more consistent in location than inferior parathyroids.

subject: Anatomy
question: A thyroglossal duct cyst moves upward with swallowing AND protrusion of the tongue. Why does tongue protrusion elevate this cyst?
options: It is attached to the hyoid bone
It is attached to the foramen cecum via the thyroglossal duct remnant
It is within the strap muscles
It is attached to the epiglottis
It is connected to the submandibular gland

rationale.text: The thyroglossal duct cyst is connected to the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue via a fibrous remnant of the thyroglossal duct. Tongue protrusion moves the foramen cecum forward and upward, elevating the cyst — a pathognomonic finding.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 20-year-old woman has a midline neck mass at the level of the hyoid bone that elevates with swallowing. Simple excision is contraindicated due to high recurrence. Which operation is the standard of care?
options: Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection
Incision and drainage with antibiotic irrigation

rationale.text: The Sistrunk procedure removes the thyroglossal duct cyst, the fibrous tract, and the central portion (body) of the hyoid bone, as the tract passes through or posterior to the hyoid. Simple excision has a very high recurrence rate.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient develops a high-pitched voice after thyroid surgery. Which nerve was likely injured and which muscle does it innervate?
options: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve; cricothyroid
Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve; arytenoid

rationale.text: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle (tensor/lengthener of vocal cords for high pitch). Its injury causes inability to raise pitch — important for singers. The RLN causes hoarseness when injured.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient develops hoarseness after thyroid surgery. Laryngoscopy shows a paralyzed vocal cord. Which nerve was injured?
options: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of superior laryngeal nerve

rationale.text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. Its injury causes hoarseness (unilateral) or aphonia and stridor (bilateral). The posterior cricoarytenoid (the only abductor of vocal cords) is also paralyzed.

subject: Anatomy
question: A thyroid ima artery, when present, typically arises from which vessel?

rationale.text: The thyroid ima artery (present in ~10% of people) arises from the brachiocephalic trunk or the arch of the aorta and ascends anterior to the trachea to supply the thyroid isthmus. It must be identified before tracheostomy.

subject: Anatomy
question: Primary hyperparathyroidism most commonly results from which pathological condition?

rationale.text: Primary hyperparathyroidism is most commonly caused by a single parathyroid adenoma (~80–85% of cases), producing excess PTH leading to hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and bone resorption.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which of the following dopaminergic pathways is responsible for regulating the secretion of prolactin?

rationale.text: The tuberoinfundibular pathway regulates prolactin secretion.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which of the following cells produce testosterone in the presence of LH?

rationale.text: Leydig cells produce testosterone under the control of LH.

subject: Anatomy
question: The site of the obliterated thyroglossal duct is called

rationale.text: Foramen cecum is the site of an obliterated thyroglossal duct.

subject: Anatomy
question: The thyroid isthmus usually crosses which of the following set of tracheal rings?

rationale.text: The thyroid isthmus usually crosses the 2nd and 3rd tracheal rings.

subject: Anatomy
question: In a thyroidectomy procedure, accidental transection of the recurrent laryngeal nerve may occur during ligation of which of the following arteries?

rationale.text: Accidental transection of the recurrent laryngeal nerve may occur during ligation of the inferior thyroid artery, leading to hoarseness.

subject: Anatomy
question: A patient with a nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma presents with bitemporal hemianopia. Where is the lesion most likely located?

rationale.text: A lesion at the optic chiasm typically presents with bitemporal hemianopia.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which of the following hypothalamic nuclei is responsible for regulating the circadian rhythm?

rationale.text: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is responsible for regulating the circadian rhythm.

subject: Anatomy
question: Which of the following zones of the adrenal gland produces androgens?

rationale.text: Androgens are produced in the zona reticularis.

subject: Anatomy
question: The adrenal medulla is embryologically derived from the

rationale.text: The adrenal medulla is embryologically derived from the neural crest.

subject: Anatomy
question: The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from which regions?
options: Entire body below the diaphragm plus left upper body
Right upper quadrant of body (right arm, right head/neck, right chest)
Entire left side of the body

rationale.text: The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper quadrant of the body: right upper limb, right head and neck, right thorax. The thoracic duct drains the rest.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 45-year-old woman with breast cancer has lymphedema of the arm after axillary node dissection. Which group of axillary lymph nodes, when removed, most commonly causes this complication?

rationale.text: Level III (apical) axillary lymph node dissection, medial to the pectoralis minor, is most likely to cause arm lymphedema as it removes the final drainage pathway to the subclavian lymph trunk.

subject: Anatomy
question: The thoracic duct drains lymph from what proportion of the body?
options: Three-quarters of the body (all except right upper quadrant)

rationale.text: The thoracic duct drains approximately three-quarters of the body — everything except the right upper quadrant (right side of head/neck, right upper limb, right hemithorax), which drains via the right lymphatic duct.

subject: Anatomy
question: The thymus develops from which pharyngeal pouch(es) and descends to which location?
options: 2nd pharyngeal pouch; descends to the neck
3rd pharyngeal pouch; descends to the anterior superior mediastinum
4th pharyngeal pouch; descends to the posterior mediastinum
1st pharyngeal pouch; remains in the neck
5th pharyngeal pouch; descends to the chest

rationale.text: The thymus develops from the ventral wing of the 3rd pharyngeal pouch and descends to the anterior superior mediastinum. It is largest in childhood and involutes after puberty.

subject: Anatomy
question: A 25-year-old woman develops muscle weakness and fatigability that improves with rest. CT chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass. Which condition is associated with a thymoma?

rationale.text: Thymoma is strongly associated with myasthenia gravis (~15–20% of MG patients have thymoma; ~30–50% of thymoma patients have MG). The thymus plays a role in the autoimmune response against acetylcholine receptors.
